---
title: "sisFFT: keeping the FFT and fixing the tail"
subtitle: "Reproducing Wilson and Keich (2017), and repairing `aggregate` on its own worst case"
---

## Introduction

@Wilson2017 computes $P = \sum_{s \ge s_0} p^{*L}(s)$, the upper tail of an $L$-fold convolution of a lattice-valued pmf, when $P$ is very small. This is the same problem as @BenRached2024 and @Asmussen2016a, on a lattice rather than a continuum, and reached from bioinformatics rather than insurance: the quantity is a $p$-value for a sequence motif, and it may need to be accurate at $10^{-150}$ because it is later multiplied by $10^{150}$ candidate alignments.

> Accurately computing very small tail probabilities of a sum of independent and identically distributed lattice-valued random variables is numerically challenging. The only general purpose algorithms that can guarantee the desired accuracy have a quadratic runtime complexity which is often too slow. While Fast Fourier Transform (FFT)-based convolutions have an essentially linear runtime complexity, they can introduce overwhelming roundoff errors. We present sisFFT (segmented iterated shifted FFT), which harnesses the speed of FFT while retaining control of the relative error of the computed tail probability.

That last sentence is why this paper is the most important of the group for `aggregate`. @BenRached2024 diagnoses the same failure and prescribes direct convolution at $O(N^2)$. This one keeps the FFT.

sisFFT combines two ideas. The first is Keich's shifted FFT, sFFT [@Keich2005]:

> It works by borrowing from large deviation theory the idea of using an exponential shift to essentially rotate $\log p$ before applying FFT-C. That is, for a suitably chosen $\theta$ this rotation will make the values $p(s)$, for $s$ close to $s_0$, the largest, and therefore FFT-C's roundoff error will be negligible with respect to them.

The second is the slicing and runtime error bound of aFFT-C [@Wilson2016a], which repairs the case where a single shift is not enough, namely when $p$ is not essentially log-concave. sisFFT chooses between shortcuts and the full path based on computable bounds, so it always knows whether its answer is trustworthy.

## What is reproducible

The main text has no tables. It has the algorithm, its proof, and timing figures. The reproducible content is a single fully specified example in the supplementary material, and it is worth more than a table because it is exact, self-contained, and lands precisely on `aggregate`'s failure mode.

From the caption to Supplementary Figure 1:

> Here $p(s) = A \cdot \exp\!\left(\frac{1}{60}s(10-s)\right)$ for $s = 0, 1, \dots, 127$, where $A$ guarantees $p$ is a pmf. In this case, the $p$-value of $s_0 = 215$ [...] is computed to be $\tilde P \approx 3 \cdot 10^{-16}$ when the convolution is performed via FFT-C. However, the true value is $P \approx 6 \cdot 10^{-154}$, hence FFT's computed value is off by more than 138 orders of magnitude.

Here $L = 2$. Because the problem is lattice-valued there is no discretization error at all, which makes this the cleanest possible probe of `aggregate`'s numerical floor: whatever goes wrong is pure roundoff.

## Setup

```{python}
#| label: setup
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy.optimize import brentq
from scipy.special import logsumexp
from aggregate import build

S_MAX, L, S0 = 127, 2, 215
s = np.arange(S_MAX + 1)
log_w = s * (10 - s) / 60
log_p = log_w - logsumexp(log_w)
p = np.exp(log_p)

print(f'dynamic range of p: {p.max():.3e} down to {p.min():.3e}')
```

## The true value, and what `aggregate` returns

Naive convolution is the reference. It is $O(N^2)$ and, as @Wilson2016a establishes, it preserves relative accuracy at every entry because a sum of non-negative products cannot cancel.

```{python}
#| label: reference
truth = np.convolve(p, p)[S0:].sum()

n = 1 << int(np.ceil(np.log2(L * S_MAX + 1)))
fftc = np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(p, n) ** L, n)[:L * S_MAX + 1][S0:].sum()

outcomes = ' '.join(str(int(k)) for k in s)
probs = ' '.join(repr(float(v)) for v in p)
obj = build(f'agg WK dfreq [{L}] dsev [{outcomes}] [{probs}]',
            log2=10, bs=1, normalize=False)
agg = float(obj.agg_density[obj.xs >= S0].sum())

pd.DataFrame([
    {'method': 'naive convolution (reference)', 'P': truth,
     'paper': '~6e-154'},
    {'method': 'FFT-C', 'P': fftc, 'paper': '~3e-16'},
    {'method': 'aggregate', 'P': agg, 'paper': 'n/a'},
])
```

The reference comes out at 6.043933e-154 against the paper's quoted $6 \times 10^{-154}$.

Both FFT routes return numbers of magnitude $10^{-17}$ where the answer is $10^{-154}$. Note that plain FFT-C comes back negative here while `aggregate` comes back positive, and the paper's own FFT-C landed positive at $3 \times 10^{-16}$. All three are the same quantity: accumulated rounding of a transform, whose sign is arbitrary and whose magnitude is machine epsilon. Only the magnitude is meaningful.

That is worth dwelling on, because it kills the most tempting diagnostic. A negative probability is a free and unambiguous failure signal, and it does appear, both here in FFT-C and in several rows on the @BenRached2024 page. But it appears only about half the time. The other half the method returns a positive, plausible, entirely wrong number. Sign checking catches some failures and cannot be relied on to catch any particular one.

```{python}
#| label: magnitude
factor = abs(agg) / truth
print(f'|agg| exceeds the true value by {factor:.3e}, '
      f'i.e. {np.log10(factor):.1f} orders of magnitude')
print('paper reports "more than 138" for its own FFT-C')
```

## Where the pmf goes wrong

The tail sum fails because the individual convolved values fail. Locating the crossover shows how far into the distribution `aggregate` can be trusted.

```{python}
#| label: crossover
exact_pmf = np.convolve(p, p)
fft_pmf = np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(p, n) ** L, n)[:L * S_MAX + 1]
rel = np.where(exact_pmf > 0,
               np.abs(fft_pmf - exact_pmf) / np.where(exact_pmf > 0, exact_pmf, 1.0),
               0.0)
bad = np.flatnonzero(rel > 1e-6)
print(f'first index with relative error above 1e-6: s = {bad[0]}, '
      f'where the true pmf is {exact_pmf[bad[0]]:.3e}')
print(f'absolute deviation from truth: median {np.median(np.abs(fft_pmf - exact_pmf)):.3e}, '
      f'max {np.abs(fft_pmf - exact_pmf).max():.3e}')
```

The departure begins where the true pmf is around $10^{-12}$ to $10^{-13}$, and the absolute deviation sits at machine epsilon regardless of position. That is the same floor found on the @BenRached2024 page from a completely different problem, and it is the general rule: FFT convolution is accurate in absolute terms at order $\varepsilon$, and therefore accurate in relative terms only while the values exceed roughly $10^{-13}$.

## The fix, applied

sFFT is the first half of sisFFT and is a few lines. Write

$$p_\theta(s) = \frac{p(s)e^{\theta s}}{M_p(\theta)}, \qquad M_p(\theta) = \sum_s p(s)e^{\theta s}.$$

The shift commutes with convolution, so $p^{*L}$ is recovered exactly:

$$p^{*L}(s) = M_p(\theta)^L\, e^{-\theta s}\, p_\theta^{*L}(s).$$

Choosing $\theta$ so the tilted mean sits at $s_0/L$ makes the values near $s_0$ the largest in the vector, so FFT roundoff is negligible relative to them. Everything is done in log space so that $e^{\theta s}$ never overflows.

```{python}
#| label: sfft
def sfft_tail(theta):
    """Keich's shifted FFT, in log space throughout."""
    log_m = logsumexp(log_p + theta * s)
    q = np.exp(log_p + theta * s - log_m)
    m = 1 << int(np.ceil(np.log2(L * S_MAX + 1)))
    conv = np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(q, m) ** L, m)[:L * S_MAX + 1]
    t = np.arange(L * S_MAX + 1)
    keep = (t >= S0) & (conv > 0)
    return np.exp(logsumexp(np.log(conv[keep]) + L * log_m - theta * t[keep]))

def tilted_mean_gap(theta):
    lw = log_p + theta * s
    w = np.exp(lw - lw.max())
    return (w @ s) / w.sum() - S0 / L

theta0 = brentq(tilted_mean_gap, 0.0, 50.0)
print(f'theta0 = {theta0:.4f}')
print(f'sFFT   = {sfft_tail(theta0):.6e}')
print(f'truth  = {truth:.6e}')
print(f'relative error = {abs(sfft_tail(theta0) / truth - 1):.3e}')
```

Thirteen significant figures, from the same FFT, at the same $O(N \log N)$ cost, on a problem where the unshifted version returns a negative number. That is the entire result.

### The shift has a working window

A single shift is not unconditionally safe, which is why sisFFT wraps it in bounds and segmentation rather than using it alone.

```{python}
#| label: window
rows = []
for th in [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, theta0, 4.0, 4.5, 5.0]:
    v = sfft_tail(th)
    rows.append({'theta': th, 'P': v, 'relative error': abs(v / truth - 1),
                 'note': 'theta0 (saddlepoint)' if th == theta0 else ''})
pd.DataFrame(rows)
```

Under-tilting leaves the target below the roundoff floor. Over-tilting pushes the tilted mass past the lattice boundary at $s = 127$, so it piles up at the top and the region near $s_0$ becomes relatively small again, recreating the original problem from the other side. The usable window here is roughly $\theta \in [3, 4]$ and $\theta_0 = 3.42$ sits inside it, but a method that has to guess $\theta$ correctly is not a method. sisFFT's contribution is that it computes bounds and therefore knows.

## Discussion

Three papers now agree on the diagnosis. @BenRached2024 proves the FFT error is bounded absolutely rather than relatively; @Wilson2016a exhibits it on adversarial pmfs; this paper exhibits it on a benign one and reproduces here to the digit. `aggregate` sits exactly on the predicted floor in all three.

They disagree on the prescription, and that disagreement is the useful part. @BenRached2024 abandons the FFT for direct convolution at $O(N^2)$, restricted to $[0, \gamma]$. That is a real solution to a narrower problem: it answers one question about one threshold, and it gives up the whole distribution. `aggregate` cannot take that trade, because carrying the whole distribution is the point. Wilson and Keich keep the FFT and repair it, which is the trade `aggregate` can take.

What this suggests for the library, in increasing order of ambition:

**Detect.** The cheapest useful change is a warning. The absolute error floor is roughly $\varepsilon \|f\|_1$, which is computable at build time with no extra work, and any returned probability below a small multiple of it is noise. Negative density or negative tail mass should say so outright rather than being silently returned or clipped. Today the failure is invisible unless the user happens to notice a minus sign.

**Bound.** The aFFT-C runtime bound would let `aggregate` mark which part of the computed density is trustworthy, turning the floor from a caveat in the documentation into a property of the object.

**Repair.** An optional tilted build. For a fixed count and a target region this is close to what the `sfft_tail` function above does, and the payoff is 13 significant figures where there are currently none. The complication is that `aggregate` supports arbitrary frequency distributions, not just a fixed $L$, and the shift interacts with the probability generating function step, so this is a design question and not a patch.

A note on scope, to keep the enthusiasm honest. Everything above concerns probabilities below about $10^{-13}$. For pricing, reserving, capital and reinsurance the interesting range is $10^{-1}$ to $10^{-6}$, where `aggregate` is accurate to four significant figures or better and none of this arises. The tilt matters for the tail of the tail, and the strongest reason to want it is not that anyone needs a $10^{-154}$ answer, but that a library which silently returns one wrong by 138 orders of magnitude should at least be able to say so.
